definition: The average value of a dataset, calculated by adding all values together and dividing by the number of values.
analogy: Like splitting a restaurant bill equally among friends. The mean tells you what each person would pay if everyone contributed the same amount.
use_in_a_sentence: The mean customer support response time last quarter was 4.2 hours, but a few extreme outliers skewed that number upward.
business_context: The mean is the most common summary statistic in business reporting, but it can be misleading when data has extreme outliers.

definition: A measure of how spread out values in a dataset are from the mean. High variance means data points are scattered widely; low variance means they cluster tightly.
analogy: Like the consistency of a basketball player's free throws. Low variance means every shot lands near the hoop; high variance means shots are all over the place.
use_in_a_sentence: The variance in daily website traffic was so high that our capacity planning team had to provision servers for peak loads rather than averages.
business_context: Understanding variance helps businesses assess risk, set realistic expectations, and plan for best-case and worst-case scenarios.

definition: The pattern that describes how values in a dataset are spread across possible outcomes — showing which values are common and which are rare.
analogy: Like a histogram of shoe sizes in a store. Most people wear sizes in the middle range, while very small and very large sizes are less common — that shape is the distribution.
use_in_a_sentence: We plotted the distribution of order values and discovered that 80% of revenue came from the top 15% of transactions.
business_context: Understanding your data's distribution is essential before applying any statistical method or machine learning algorithm.

definition: A statistical measure of how strongly two variables move together. Positive correlation means they increase together; negative means one increases as the other decreases.
analogy: Like noticing that ice cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in summer. They are correlated — they move together — but one does not cause the other.
use_in_a_sentence: We found a strong correlation between email open rates and subsequent purchases, which helped prioritize our marketing budget.
business_context: Correlation is useful for identifying relationships in data, but remember: correlation does not imply causation. Further analysis is always needed.

definition: When a model learns the training data too well — including its noise and quirks — and performs poorly on new, unseen data. The model memorizes rather than generalizes.
analogy: Like a student who memorizes every answer in the practice exam but cannot solve new problems because they never learned the underlying concepts.
use_in_a_sentence: Our model achieved 99% accuracy on training data but only 65% on new data — a classic sign of overfitting that we addressed by adding more diverse training examples.
business_context: Overfitting is one of the most common pitfalls in ML projects. It gives a false sense of confidence during development that collapses in production.

definition: When a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the data, resulting in poor performance on both training data and new data.
analogy: Like trying to describe a detailed landscape painting using only three crayons. The tools are too limited to capture the complexity of what you are looking at.
use_in_a_sentence: The linear model was underfitting our highly seasonal sales data, so we switched to a model that could capture non-linear trends.
business_context: Underfitting usually means you need a more sophisticated model or better features — it is the opposite problem from overfitting.

definition: A measure of how spread out data points are from the mean, expressed in the same units as the data. It is the square root of variance and is easier to interpret in real-world terms.
analogy: Like the typical distance commuters live from the office. If the standard deviation is 5 miles, most people live within about 5 miles of work, though some live farther.
use_in_a_sentence: Delivery times averaged 3 days with a standard deviation of 0.5 days, meaning most packages arrived within 2.5 to 3.5 days.
business_context: Standard deviation appears constantly in business reporting, quality control, and SLA definitions. It tells you what 'normal variation' looks like.

definition: Of all the items the model predicted as positive, the percentage that actually were positive. High precision means few false alarms.
analogy: Like a spam filter's pickiness. High precision means almost every email it flags as spam really is spam — it rarely bothers you with a legitimate email marked as junk.
use_in_a_sentence: Our fraud model has 95% precision, meaning when it flags a transaction as fraudulent, it is correct 95% of the time.
business_context: Precision matters most when false positives are costly — blocking legitimate transactions, flagging innocent people, or wasting investigators' time on false leads.

definition: Of all the items that actually were positive, the percentage the model successfully identified. High recall means few cases slip through the cracks.
analogy: Like a security checkpoint trying to catch every prohibited item. High recall means almost nothing dangerous gets through, even if some harmless items get flagged too.
use_in_a_sentence: The cancer screening model achieves 98% recall — it catches nearly every true positive — though some healthy patients get flagged for follow-up testing.
business_context: Recall matters most when missing a positive case is dangerous or expensive — medical diagnoses, security threats, or critical defects in manufacturing.

definition: A single metric that balances precision and recall into one number between 0 and 1. It is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when you need both to be reasonably high.
analogy: Like a restaurant rating that balances food quality and service. A place with amazing food but terrible service (or vice versa) gets a mediocre combined score — you want both to be good.
use_in_a_sentence: We optimized for F1 score because our use case required a balance between catching fraud (recall) and not blocking legitimate customers (precision).
business_context: F1 score is the go-to metric when accuracy alone is misleading, especially with imbalanced datasets where one class is much rarer than the other.

definition: A range of values that is likely to contain the true answer, along with a confidence level (often 95%). It expresses uncertainty — wider intervals mean less certainty.
analogy: Like a weather forecast saying 'between 70 and 80 degrees tomorrow.' The forecaster is not giving one exact number but a range they are fairly confident about.
use_in_a_sentence: Our A/B test showed a 12% improvement in conversion with a 95% confidence interval of 8% to 16%, so we are confident the new design is genuinely better.
business_context: Confidence intervals help decision-makers understand how much to trust a result. A narrow interval means strong evidence; a wide one means more data may be needed.

definition: A data point that is dramatically different from the rest of the dataset — unusually high, unusually low, or otherwise abnormal compared to the general pattern.
analogy: Like one student scoring 100% on a test where everyone else scored between 40% and 70%. That score is so different from the group that it stands out and may need special attention.
use_in_a_sentence: A single $50,000 order skewed our average order value, so we identified it as an outlier and reported the median alongside the mean for a more accurate picture.
business_context: Outliers can distort statistics and confuse models. They may represent errors, fraud, or genuinely unusual events — the key is investigating them rather than ignoring them.

definition: The process of rescaling data so that different features are on a comparable scale — for example, converting all values to a 0-to-1 range. This prevents features with large numbers from dominating the model.
analogy: Like converting different currencies to a common one before comparing prices. A salary of 5,000,000 yen and 40,000 dollars look very different until you normalize them to the same scale.
use_in_a_sentence: After normalizing our features, the model stopped over-weighting revenue (measured in millions) relative to customer count (measured in hundreds).
business_context: Normalization is a standard preprocessing step. Skipping it can cause models to produce poor results simply because one feature had bigger numbers than others.
